Work / Daybook / Independent prototype

Daybook.
Built for the next state.

A booking interface is the beginning. Daybook explores what happens when a request needs to wait, a connection fails, and the system has to recover without doing the same work twice.

The product

A small booking. A whole system behind it.

I built Daybook as an independent working prototype for this site. It connects a usable HTML product to a spatial view of its interface, request queue, simulated API and sample device.

Open Daybook All independent work

The question

What happens after the booking button?

A convincing screen can hide an unreliable workflow. A booking needs valid input and an available slot. A disconnected service needs a visible queue. A retry needs to deliver the original request, not create another one.

Daybook brings those decisions into one local system. The interface remains usable without 3D; the spatial view makes the current system state easier to inspect.

Working scope

The behaviour is the evidence.

Validated bookings

Local validation checks the guest name and selected slot. A slot already held by a booking cannot be booked again.

Visible delivery state

Bookings remain pending when the simulated API is disconnected. Connecting it processes eligible requests while retaining their identity.

Controlled faults

Simulated API and device faults interrupt delivery. The affected request stays in the system rather than disappearing behind a success message.

Repair & replay

Recovery retries pending requests. Idempotent handling prevents an already delivered request from being delivered again.

An inspectable trail

Local events record the important transitions. The booking product and 3D system reflect the same domain state.

A public build artifact

A share link restores allowlisted sample settings. A PNG build card captures the public system configuration, excluding guest names, booking records and inquiry drafts.

Architecture & responsibility

One state. More than one view.

  • Domain logic owns the workflow

    Booking validation, request identity, queue transitions and recovery belong to local application state, not to an animation timeline.

  • HTML owns the product interaction

    Native form controls, visible records and explicit feedback carry the booking flow. The canvas is an additional view, not the only way to operate the product.

  • Three.js explains the system

    The spatial composition responds to the same connection and fault state as the interface. Reduced motion, pause and a static fallback keep the product independent of the spectacle.

  • Sharing has a separate boundary

    Only public configuration is serialized. Restored examples use synthetic sample state instead of copying the visitor's private booking data.

Scope & limits

A prototype, not a production claim.

All bookings, queue processing, API responses and device events are local simulations. There is no backend, real appointment, payment, external notification or connected production device.

The demo has three fixed sample slots. Request records exist only in this page's memory and are cleared by reset or reload; shared setups restore a synthetic example, not your records.

This is my independent product experiment, not commissioned client work. It demonstrates a bounded workflow; it does not establish production reliability, security certification or a measured business result.

A production version would need server-side validation and durable storage, authentication, real integration contracts, monitoring and testing against the agreed deployment environment.
